## Abstract

Whole-brain simulations built on the fly connectome make predictions of the form "silence this cell type and that behaviour disappears". Every such prediction rests on one brain: one female (FlyWire) and one male (MaleCNS). Synapse counts between the same pair of cell types differ between brains and between the two hemispheres of one brain, so a prediction carried by a handful of connections may or may not survive in another animal, and no published simulation says which. FlyBnB is a dataset built to say which. It silences and activates every annotated cell type under a battery of sensory stimuli, records the output of all descending neurons, and repeats every result in one hundred synthetic individuals whose wiring varies as much as the two hemispheres of a real brain do. The execution semantics are integer and bit-exact, so each row of the dataset carries a digest that anybody can recompute; rows are executed redundantly on a peer-to-peer network of browser nodes and settled on BNB Chain, with a fraud proof for a wrong result. The individuals are hosted by the people who hold them, and the dataset acknowledges them (Appendix A). This draft reports the two pilots that the programme depends on: whether calibrated wiring variability moves a circuit phenotype by more than the assay's own noise, and whether a phenotype is transmitted by the collection's cross so that selection can move it.

## 1. Introduction

A connectome is a sample of one. The published simulations of the adult fly brain take a single wiring diagram, turn synapse counts into weights, and ask what the network does when a population of neurons is driven or removed. Several of their predictions have been confirmed in the animal, which is what makes the approach worth taking seriously. What none of them reports is how a prediction depends on the particular brain it was computed on. The question is not rhetorical: comparisons between the available connectomes, and between the left and right side of one brain, show that the number of synapses between two cell types varies considerably, and connections near any inclusion threshold appear and disappear.

We became interested in this through one result. In the female brain, two ascending neurons silence a descending neuron (DNge145) that would otherwise respond to sound; deleting four direct connections abolishes the effect and keeping only those four preserves it. Four connections is not many. Whether the effect holds in another individual is a question about those four counts and about everything else that feeds the same cell, and it can only be answered by building other individuals and looking.

FlyBnB makes this the unit of the dataset. A row is one whole-brain run: a perturbation, a stimulus, an individual, a stimulus seed. The individual axis is what is new. The second property we care about is that a row can be checked. A resource that will be cited for years should not depend on trusting whoever computed it, so the simulator is defined in integer arithmetic, its result is a hash, and the network that produces the rows executes each one more than once and can prove a wrong one wrong.

## 2. Methods

### 2.1 Brains and execution semantics

The female brain is FlyWire v783 (139,255 neurons); the male brain is MaleCNS v1.0. Each is exported as a `FLYBRAINv2` payload: a list of (presynaptic, postsynaptic, signed synapse count) records sorted by postsynaptic neuron, content-addressed by the Merkle root of its 4 KiB tiles (`model_id`). Simulation is `aigg:exec:int-lif:v1`, a leaky integrate-and-fire network in Q16 fixed point with a synaptic conductance, a refractory period, and no background noise. A stimulus is a set of neurons that emit hash-driven spikes at about 150 Hz; the only randomness in a run is that spike train, fixed by a seed. One step is 0.1 ms and a standard run is 5,000 steps. The result of a run is the vector of per-neuron spike counts, and its digest is the Keccak-256 hash of that vector. Three implementations (a reference, a sparse reference that visits only the outgoing records of neurons that spiked, and the WebAssembly kernel the browser nodes run) produce identical digests.

### 2.2 Individuals

An individual is the base wiring with every synapse count redrawn. A count `c` is replaced by a draw from a negative binomial distribution with mean proportional to `c` and a dispersion that depends on `c`; the dispersion table was fitted to the differences between the left and right hemisphere of the same brain for homologous connections, and the variance attributed to one individual is half the variance of a left-right pair. Draws are a pure function of a seed and the (pre, post) pair, in 256-bit fixed point, and are implemented identically in JavaScript, Python and Solidity. Individuals are laid out in place on a base that keeps connections of two synapses or more; a record whose drawn count falls below five is kept with weight zero, so connections can cross the threshold in both directions and an individual's identity can be challenged on-chain one record at a time. An individual is published as a recipe of a few hundred bytes (`FLYDELTAv3`), and offspring are crosses of two recipes with mutation.

### 2.3 Stimuli, perturbations and readouts

A stimulus is a named set of sensory neurons defined from the annotations. A perturbation is either a set of neurons whose output is forced to zero (silencing), a set added to the stimulus (activation), or an edit to individual connections. The readout is not chosen in advance: the full spike-count vector is stored sparsely, and the 1,303 descending neurons of the female brain are the default behavioural readout. Because the simulator is deterministic and has no background activity, silencing a neuron that does not spike in a given run provably leaves the run unchanged, so the silencing atlas needs only the cell types that are active in that individual under that stimulus; the remaining cells of the table are filled with the digest of the unperturbed run.

### 2.4 Execution and verification

Rows are posted as tasks to a network of browser nodes that keep the brains resident in memory. Each task is executed by more than one node chosen by sortition; identical digests settle the task, and a disagreement, or a challenge by anybody who recomputes a settled row and gets a different digest, is resolved on-chain by bisection down to a single synaptic term. Until batched tasks make that economical at the scale of the atlas, rows are generated offline with the sparse reference and published with their digests, and settlement on the network accumulates as independent replication.

## 3. Pilot: do phenotypes differ between individuals?

The atlas is only worth building if calibrated wiring variability moves a phenotype by more than the noise of the assay. The pilot measures that and nothing else. Founders are in-place individuals on the female base. Each is run under the same stimulus seeds with two stimuli: both ears' Johnston's organ neurons, and the same with the two gate neurons added. Individual 0 is the base wiring itself and reproduces the published reference run digit for digit. Because every individual sees the same spike trains, variance separates into a between-individual component, a between-seed component and their interaction, and the intraclass correlation is the repeatability of the assay; as the wiring of a founder is its genotype, it is also the broad-sense heritability of the assay in this population.

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED: pilot -->
**Design.** 100 founders × 10 stimulus seeds × 2 stimuli, 5,000 steps each (2000 runs, plus the base wiring).

**Wiring.** A founder keeps 2,689,194 connections of five synapses or more (base: 2,700,513) and 34,707,381 synapses (base: 34,153,566). About 798,495 base connections fall below the threshold and 787,176 rise above it: the totals are stationary, the membership is not.

**Reading.** The intraclass correlation of a single half-second assay runs from 0.36 (whole-brain spikes, sound only (0.5 s)) to 0.89 (giant fibre, sound + gate); 9 of 11 phenotypes are at 0.6 or above, and averaged over the seeds every phenotype is at 0.87 or above. Where the ICC is high, an individual's phenotype is a property of its wiring that one run measures; the numbers say which readouts that is true of, and it is not true of all of them to the same degree.

**The gate.** The published result on the base wiring is that the gate silences DNge145. Across founders the gate reduces DNge145 on average, but complete silencing is not the rule: 39% of runs are fully silenced, 8% of individuals are silenced under every seed, and 37% are never fully silenced. The four direct gate connections carry 22, 33, 29, 30 synapses in the base and sum to 102 ± 23 across founders (52 to 165); the correlation between that sum and the residual DNge145 activity under the gate is -0.27, so the direct connections alone do not explain who leaks.
<!-- END GENERATED: pilot -->

What the pilot does not show. It says nothing about narrow-sense heritability under the cross, which needs parent-offspring pairs. It covers two stimuli and one sex. And the variability it applies is a model: every connection is redrawn independently, whereas real differences between animals are probably correlated along a neuron and a lineage; the left-right and female-male comparisons of Section 5 are there to test that.

## 3a. Breeding pilot: is a phenotype transmitted, and does selection move it?

Every individual gets the same **standard battery** (`flybnb/battery/`): 13 sensory stimuli × 3 seeds, the output of all 1,303 descending neurons. That is what makes the perturbation atlas, an association analysis over wiring, and a selection experiment three readings of one table. The third has the most to prove, so it was piloted first.

The assay is deterministic: for fixed seeds a phenotype is a function of the wiring and of nothing else, so all of its variance between individuals is genetic. What is not given is how much of it a parent passes on. Under the collection's cross an offspring takes each connection from one parent or the other, and then one connection in eight is redrawn around the base. An additive phenotype therefore regresses on the midparent with slope 7/8 = 0.875; that is an expectation for additive phenotypes and not a bound. A slope well below it means that part of the phenotype lives in interactions between connections, which recombination breaks up.

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED: breeding -->
**Design.** 100 founders, 100 randomly mated offspring, and 50 + 50 offspring of two divergent selection lines; every individual under the full battery (39 runs). 674 phenotypes: named cell types, per-stimulus totals, and every descending cell type that is active in at least half of the founders.

**Phenotypes are transmitted.** The midparent regression slope, the narrow-sense heritability under this cross, has median 0.67 (quartiles 0.55 to 0.80); 82% of phenotypes are above 0.5. Against the additive expectation of 0.875 (slope ± 2 SE): 248 phenotypes are clearly below it, 422 are consistent with it, 4 clearly above. So for about 37% of phenotypes a measurable part lives in interactions between connections, which recombination breaks up.

**Selection works, in one generation.** Selected trait: DNge145 | sound (founder mean 9.55). The high line's parents were 8.89 above the mean and their offspring 7.01 above it; the low line's parents 7.18 below and their offspring 5.43 below. Realised heritability 0.77 (high 0.79, low 0.76); the midparent regression gives 1.06 ± 0.12. The two lines end 2.09 founder standard deviations apart.

**What else moved.** Of 674 phenotypes, 14 differ between the two lines at a false discovery rate of 0.05, and 10 of those are not DNge145 phenotypes: DNg24 | sound (-0.99 SD); DNge041 | head_bristle (-0.83 SD); DNg38 | sugar (+0.75 SD); DNp35 | sound (-0.75 SD); DNpe020 | eye_bristle (-0.67 SD); DNg35 | eye_bristle (-0.64 SD). Selection on one response is mostly specific, and not entirely. The one trade-off that matters here is inside the selected circuit: the line bred for a strong response to sound also leaks more through the gate (DNge145 under `sound_gate`: 6.45 against 0.93).

What this does not show. The cross is a model of inheritance over connections, not the genetics of a fly: a real animal inherits developmental programs, not synapse counts. What the pilot measures is the shape of the phenotype landscape around a real connectome under a recombination that the collection's contracts can verify. One generation is not a selection experiment; whether the response continues, plateaus, or costs other behaviours is what further generations are for.

## 4. The dataset

One row per run: brain, individual (recipe hash and `model_id`), perturbation, stimulus, seed, steps, digest, total spikes, active neurons, and the sparse spike-count vector. The pilot split is the runs of Section 3. The dataset is prepared for the Hugging Face Hub; the card, the schema and the export script are in [`flybnb/dataset/`](../../flybnb/dataset/).

## 5. Planned analyses

**H1, the distribution of robustness.** Of the perturbation effects detected on the base wiring, what fraction replicate in most individuals, and is robustness bimodal or continuous.

**H2, robustness from wiring.** Whether an effect carried by many parallel, high-count connections is robust and one carried by a few near-threshold connections is fragile, which would give a robustness index that needs no simulation.

**H3, across hemispheres and sexes.** The two hemispheres of one brain are two natural individuals, and non-dimorphic circuits should agree between the female and the male brain. Effects that are robust across synthetic individuals should agree across these more often than fragile ones; if they do not, the variability model is missing the structure of real individual differences.

**H4, against experiment.** Published silencing and activation phenotypes are mapped onto rows. The prediction is that they are recovered more often among robust rows, and the dataset ships a ranked list of robust, large, untested predictions.

## 6. Limitations

The simulator has no neuromodulation, no gap junctions and no cell-type-specific parameters: the atlas measures the phenotypes of this model. Driving a set of sensory neurons at a fixed rate is not a natural stimulus. Activity is sparse, a few hundred neurons in half a second, so many perturbations have no measurable effect under a given stimulus, and absence of effect must not be read as absence of function. The idea is not new: activation and silencing predictions have been made for selected circuits. What FlyBnB adds is completeness, the individual axis, and rows that can be recomputed.

## 7. Data and code availability

Everything the pilot needs is public. The pilot's code, its results (every run with its digest) and the dataset export are in [`flybnb/`](../../flybnb/) of this repository, with the content addresses of the two brain payloads and how to export them from the FlyWire release. Contracts, relayer and the browser node: `jianmliu/aigg-bnb` and `jianmliu/aigg-porw`. Payload formats, the individual sampler and its test vectors: `aigg-porw`. The research proposal is [`proposal.md`](proposal.md).
